query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX HEAs, the ability of the alloy to form and retain a stable, coherent protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C is determined by the nature of the X element: Al and Si promote the segregation of these elements to the surface to form a continuous, slow-growing, coherent Al2O3 or SiO2 scale, whereas Mn encourages the formation of a porous, less adherent oxide that is prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys with controlled X substitutions (X = Al, Si, or Mn) in either a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloys to high-temperature conditions (above 900 °C) in a controlled oxidative or corrosive environment.
generation.conditions: Temperature above 900 °C with well-controlled oxidizing/corrosive atmospheres; comparisons made under identical thermal cycling and environmental conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of a coherent, continuous oxide scale mediated by the surface segregation of Al or Si leading to the formation of dense, low-diffusivity oxide films (Al2O3 or SiO2) versus the discontinuous, less adherent oxide phases formed when Mn is present.
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, the alloying element X diffuses and segregates to the surface. In the case of Al or Si, the resulting oxide (alumina or silica) forms a dense, coherent layer due to its slow oxygen diffusion kinetics and good adhesion to the substrate. In contrast, Mn segregates to form oxides that tend to be porous and mechanically unstable, leading to cracking and eventual spallation under thermal stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Al or Si will form a stable and coherent protective oxide layer that persists with minimal spallation during exposure, while alloys with Mn will develop unstable oxide layers characterized by microstructural discontinuities, cracking, and spallation.
generation.baseline: The comparative baseline is provided by Mn-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys, which are expected to form less protective oxide layers.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to HEAs maintained in single- or multiphase solid-solution states and exposed to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres. Effects outside these conditions are not considered in this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: The precise concentration thresholds of Al or Si required to achieve the stable oxide layer and any potential modifying effects due to multiphase microstructures remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Si, and Mn at matched overall compositions and process histories. Expose all samples to temperatures above 900 °C in an identical, well-controlled oxidative (or corrosive) atmosphere for a fixed duration. Characterize the surface oxide layers using microscopy (SEM/TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and adhesion tests.
measurements: Presence and phase composition of oxide films (Al2O3, SiO2, Mn-oxides)
Microstructural integrity (coherence, porosity, cracking) of the oxide scales
Adhesion strength and spallation incidence during thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if Mn-containing alloys exhibit oxide layers that are as continuous, coherent, and stable as those formed on Al- or Si-containing alloys under identical conditions, or if the protective oxide layers in Al/Si variants do not demonstrate superior adherence and stability compared to the Mn variant.
